newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: TENNIS-PAST GREATS WARY OF LIFE IN THE FAST LANE.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-PAST GREATS WARY OF LIFE IN THE FAST LANE.

text.p: 'Don't blink or you'll miss it' will be the theme of this year's Wimbledon, and that bothers many of tennis's legendary names who mourn the decline of touch play in the men's game.
Spectators may gasp at the huge power generated by the big-servers and enjoy studying the speeds displayed on the radar monitor almost as much as the point itself.
But to names such as Bjorn Borg, Guillermo Vilas and Andres Gomez -- all Grand Slam title winners -- the fun should be in watching the players on the court, not the scoreboard.

"Fortunately there is only one major tournament on grass," said Gomez, winner of the 1990 French Open. "It (Wimbledon) is still the biggest tournament of all, but I don't think people enjoy it as much as before."
If last weekend's Wimbledon warm-up at Queen's Club was any indication, Gomez may well be proved right.

In a match which demonstrated how one-dimensional the modern game can be on grass, Australian Mark Philippoussis beat Croat Goran Ivanisevic in less than an hour. The match produced only five points which featured rallies of more than four shots as the pair sent down 27 aces between them.

Philippoussis holds the record for the fastest serve measured on the circuit at 229 kph, while Greg Rusedski of Britain, runner-up with 223.7 kph, is also given much more of a chance during the Wimbledon fortnight than he would on most other surfaces.
"This is the future of men's tennis. The fans better get used to it," acknowledged Bjorn Borg, a five-time winner of what is arguably tennis's most cherished event.
Borg believes that with players becoming stronger, better-trained and with the advances in equipment, there is only one way for the game to go -- faster.
But he is quick to add that his odds-on favourite to win the event is not the hardest server, but the game's best finesse player Pete Sampras.

"Pete would be my choice with his strong all-round skills, but there are a lot of evenly-matched players so there could still be a lot of upsets," Borg, currently competing on the ATP Senior's Tour said.

Several top players naturally suited to slower surfaces, such as Spaniards Sergi Bruguera, the French Open finalist, Alex Corretja, Felix Mantilla and Alberto Berasategui have already decided to cut their losses, and have pulled out or declined to enter Wimbledon.
Their absence, to some people's chagrin, leaves the field open to the big hitters.
"There were less guys in our time who could just rely on hitting the ball hard and not have to play points," said Gene Mayer, ranked fourth in the world in 1980.

"One of the difficulties in today's game is that people can't relate to it. If they see points going on, they can see what it's like and understand the game, as opposed to watching someone who just hits aces and puts the ball away.
"That's unfortunate and maybe the reason why women's tennis is gaining again in appeal. At least people can see what's going on. It's not just one shot and the point is over."
